overview: Malacca, founded about 1400 by Parameswara, a prince from Palembang, became within a century the greatest port of Asia, where the monsoons met. Its sultans made Islam and Malay the faith and language of the archipelago's trade.

items.text: Ships from China, Gujarat, Bengal, Arabia, Java and the Spice Islands met at Malacca to exchange cloth, spices, tin, gold and porcelain.
Tomé Pires, writing just after the conquest, counted 84 languages spoken in the city and wrote that whoever was lord of Malacca had his hand on the throat of Venice.
Zheng He's fleets called at Malacca from 1405, and the sultanate sent missions to the Ming court.
The ruler adopted Islam around 1414, taking the name Iskandar Shah; Malacca became a center from which Islam spread to Java and the islands.
The Undang-Undang Melaka, the laws of Malacca, and the Malay Annals were written in Malay in the Arabic script.
Malay spread as the lingua franca of maritime Southeast Asia and became Malaysian and Indonesian.
Malacca's laws and court customs set the model for the Malay sultanates.

fall.text: Afonso de Albuquerque took the city in August 1511 after a month's fighting; the sultan fled and his heirs founded Johor.
